paper: Erdelez & Makri (2020) Information encountering re-encountered: A conceptual re-examination of serendipity in the context of information acquisition, Journal of Documentation 76(3) 731-751
why: Defines information encountering as chance finding of information while looking for other information, with a temporal model of the encounter inside a search task. Would state the 'stumbled on something else while searching' half. Author accepted version at openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/23843.

paper: What Makes Mothers Decide (Not) to Become Entrepreneurs? Unpacking the Role of Time and Money in Parental Leave Policies (2025), Journal of Management Studies
why: Excerpt: childbirth, as a transitional life event, reshapes roles and time and influences the likelihood of entering entrepreneurship.

paper: Haynie & Shepherd (2011) Toward a theory of discontinuous career transition: investigating career transitions necessitated by traumatic life events, Journal of Applied Psychology
why: Abstract: disabled veterans rebuild 'foundational assumptions about the world, humanity, and self' before a new career path, a slow inner change after trauma.

paper: Davidsson, Recker & von Briel (2020) External Enablement of New Venture Creation: A Framework, Academy of Management Perspectives 34(3) 311-332
why: Source of the onset dimension (suddenness, predictability) and the triggering / shaping / outcome-enhancing roles, as reported by Klyver & Nielsen and Salvi et al.; not held, so its own wording is unread.

paper: Kimjeon & Davidsson (2021/2022) External Enablers of Entrepreneurship: A Review and Agenda for Accumulation of Strategically Actionable Knowledge, Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
why: Open-access excerpt: 'The two dimensions of onset are gradual-sudden and predictable-unpredictable', with environmental degradation as a gradual example; would give a direct statement of gradual change as an enabler.

paper: Cutolo & Grimaldi (2023) I wasn't expecting that: how engaging with digital platforms can turn leisure passion into entrepreneurial aspirations, JBV Insights
why: Title/abstract: unexpected entrepreneurial turn from platform activity built for leisure; may tie a prior following to chance.

paper: Preller, Breugst & Patzelt (2023) Team resilience building in response to co-founder exits, JBV
why: For the 'partner vanished' half: how ventures respond to a co-founder leaving; open access.

paper: Murphy (2011) A 2 x 2 Conceptual Foundation for Entrepreneurial Discovery Theory, Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice 35(2)
why: Separates 'eureka' (high serendipity, high deliberation) from 'serendipitous discovery' (high serendipity, low deliberation); the source that says whether a sudden insight counts as serendipity.

paper: Stevenson, Allen and Wang (2022) Failed but validated? The effect of market validation on persistence and performance after a crowdfunding failure, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Validation without a successful sale (failed campaign that still shows demand); carried over from round 2, still not held.

paper: Jabbouri, Whittle, Truong and Schneckenberg (2025) Narrative Switching in Entrepreneurial Failure Accounts, British Journal of Management 36(4)
why: Entrepreneurs suddenly change the story they tell about a failure; may document switching from setback to positive framing.

paper: Murray, Cohen & Iqbal (2026) How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal
why: Abstract names 'normalizing setbacks and resolutions' as a practice ventures use when setbacks are exposed; the closest statement found, though aimed at stakeholders rather than the founder's own account.

paper: Cardon, Stevens & Potter (2011) Misfortunes or mistakes? Cultural sensemaking of entrepreneurial failure, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Sets misfortune against mistake in accounts of failure; would show whether a third 'normal hazard' framing appears.

paper: Schweisfurth & Greul (2024) Unexpected Interruptions, Idle Time, and Creativity: Evidence from a Natural Experiment, Organization Science 35(1) 116-137
why: Abstract: an unexpected supply-shortage stoppage that created idle time raised employees' ideas by 58%; planned breaks did not. Closest to an unplanned idle day making room for new ideas. Green OA copy at research.utwente.nl.

paper: Khurana, Lee & de Castro (2026) The impact of workers' compensation laws on entrepreneurial activity, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal
why: Abstract: uses exogenous shocks to workers' free time (injury; Illinois law change) and finds free time, with liquidity, raises entrepreneurial activity. States 'free time is a resource for founding'.

paper: Garud, Gehman & Giuliani (2014) Contextualizing entrepreneurial innovation: A narrative perspective, Research Policy
why: Named in the brief; argues narratives give retrospective coherence to entrepreneurial journeys. Not held.

paper: Lough (2022) Do Founders Attribute Their Success to Skill or Luck? Research Square preprint
why: OA excerpt: among founders' themes are 'luck as circumstances of privilege, most prominently including where the founder was born' and 'the luck of being born to a particular family or parentage'. Still framed as luck; preprint, not peer reviewed.

paper: Greenwood and Gopal (2015) Research Note: Tigerblood: Newspapers, Blogs, and the Founding of Information Technology Firms, Information Systems Research
why: Treats increases in newspaper and blog coverage as an outside shock to entrepreneurship.

paper: Erdelez (1999) Information Encountering: It's More Than Just Bumping into Information, Bulletin of the American Society for Information Science 25(3) 26-29
why: Founding statement of information encountering during search for other information (256 citing statements in scite).

paper: Tran (2026) Self-Employment Entry Across Family Transitions: Household Capability Reallocation Over the Life Course, Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
why: Abstract: marriage and childbirth are positively associated with entry into self-employment; identical life events produce different entry responses by role and life stage.

paper: Schjoedt & Shaver (2007) Deciding on an Entrepreneurial Career: A Test of the Pull and Push Hypotheses Using the Panel Study of Entrepreneurial Dynamics Data, Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
why: Abstract tests whether job dissatisfaction pushes people toward an entrepreneurial career.

paper: Noorderhaven, Thurik, Wennekers & van Stel (2004) The Role of Dissatisfaction and per Capita Income in Explaining Self-Employment across 15 European Countries, Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice
why: Abstract: dissatisfaction as a push 'displacement' toward self-employment.

paper: Yitshaki & Kropp (2016) Motivations and Opportunity Recognition of Social Entrepreneurs, Journal of Small Business Management
why: Abstract: some founders were pulled by past or current life events, others pushed by job dissatisfaction and a search for meaning.

paper: Maitlis (2009) Who am I now? Sensemaking and identity in posttraumatic growth, in Exploring Positive Identities and Organizations
why: Cited by Shepherd & Williams (2020) for post-traumatic growth; gradual identity change after a life-altering event.

paper: Tang, Kacmar & Busenitz (2012) Entrepreneurial alertness in the pursuit of new opportunities, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Defines alertness as alert scanning and search, association, and evaluation; would anchor the disposition in entrepreneurship.

paper: Cheng, de Regt & Young (2024) The influencer-entrepreneurship journey: a model of staged progression, Psychology & Marketing
why: Abstract: influencers build 'attentional capital' over stages ending in 'influence monetization'; open access (cc-by).

paper: Roccapriore & Pollock (2023) I don't need a degree, I've got abs: influencer warmth and competence, communication mode, and stakeholder engagement on social media, AMJ
why: Cited by D'Oria as the core 'entrepreneur-as-influencer' study of how influencers grow a following.

paper: Guinez-Cabrera & Aqueveque (2022) on influencers as digital entrepreneurs (cited by D'Oria; journal not verified)
why: D'Oria cites it for 'amass a substantial following and creates entrepreneurial opportunities to monetize such attention'.

paper: Bao, Wei & Di Benedetto (2020) Identifying the tacit entrepreneurial opportunity of latent customer needs in an emerging economy: experiential versus vicarious market learning, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal 14(3) 444-469
why: Excerpts say latent needs arise when customers meet unexpected problems, go unnoticed by the customers themselves, and are identified through experiential (hands-on) market learning; Haier 'happened to identify' farmers' unanticipated need. Closest to 'only founders close to customers notice'.

paper: Mitchell, Levin & Krumboltz (1999) Planned happenstance: constructing unexpected career opportunities, Journal of Counseling & Development
why: Abstract: chance plays an important role in everyone's career; unplanned events become opportunities.

paper: Peterson & Meckler (2001) Cuban-American entrepreneurs: chance, complexity and chaos, Organization Studies
why: Abstract: traces chance through one entrepreneur's personal career history.

paper: Engel, van Burg & Kleijn (2017) Past career in future thinking: how career management practices shape entrepreneurial decision making, SEJ
why: Excerpt: career practices that predate entry shape later founding; open access.

paper: Dougherty, Neubert & Park (2013) A Religious Profile of American Entrepreneurs, Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion
why: Entrepreneurs see God as more personal and pray more often than non-entrepreneurs; background for providence accounts, not a founder-narrative finding.

paper: Weiner (1985) An attributional theory of achievement motivation and emotion, Psychological Review
why: Source of the ability/effort/task difficulty/luck scheme cited by Liu & de Rond; would show product or team credit as task or external causes outside luck and effort.

paper: Parnell, Dent & O'Regan (2012) Managing Performance in a Volatile Environment: Contrasting Perspectives on Luck and Causality, British Journal of Management
why: Practitioner accounts of luck and causality; the law-of-probability view of luck averaging out is close to the 'statistics' account. OA green.

paper: Gable, Hopper and Schooler (2019) When the Muses Strike: Creative Ideas of Physicists and Writers Routinely Occur During Mind Wandering, Psychological Science 30(3)
why: One fifth of significant ideas arise during unrelated activity and mind wandering, often as 'aha' moments; matches ideas on the golf course or in the shower.

paper: Ovington, Saliba, Moran, Goldring and MacDonald (2015/2018) Do People Really Have Insights in the Shower? The When, Where and Who of the Aha! Moment, Journal of Creative Behavior 52(1)
why: Documents where and when aha moments occur, including the shower.

paper: Gans, Stern & Wu (2019) Foundations of entrepreneurial strategy, Strategic Management Journal 40(5) 736-756
why: Abstract: entrepreneurs face many alternatives that cannot be pursued at once, so must adopt a process for choosing; may give a general statement that saying no to options is central.

paper: Sieger, Zellweger, Nason & Clinton (2011) Portfolio entrepreneurship in family firms: a resource-based perspective, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal 5(4)
why: Excerpt: a founder's strong industry reputation brought invitations to consortia and projects in other industries; 'reputation can attract outsiders who are looking for partners for their own entrepreneurial ventures'. States reputation-driven inbound opportunities for entrepreneurs.

paper: Kundu, Anderson & Ramdas (2024) Disruptions, Redundancy Strategies, and Performance of Small Firms: Evidence from Uganda, Management Science
why: Abstract: managerial disruptions that take the entrepreneur-owner away from the business significantly cut monthly sales and sales growth.

paper: Eddleston, Sieger & Chirico (2025) The King Is Dead - Long Live Who? A Family and Firm Embeddedness Perspective on Succession after the CEO-Owner's Sudden Death, Journal of Management Studies
why: Abstract: an SME's financial health gets progressively worse after the owner's sudden death. This is the founder's own death, not a loss in the founder's life, so at best adjacent.

paper: Georgellis, Sessions & Tsitsianis (2005) Windfalls, wealth, and the transition to self-employment, Small Business Economics
why: Abstract: windfall gains raise the probability of moving into self-employment; general entry, not chance opportunities.

paper: Hurst & Lusardi (2004) Liquidity constraints, household wealth, and entrepreneurship, Journal of Political Economy
why: Abstract: wealth matters for entry only at the top of the distribution; a counterpoint.

paper: Bellon, Cookson, Gilje & Heimer (2021) Personal wealth, self-employment, and business ownership, Review of Financial Studies
why: Abstract: cash windfalls extend self-employment spells; effects depend on motives.

paper: Wang, Song and Zhao (2014) Legitimacy and the Value of Early Customers, Journal of Product Innovation Management 31(5)
why: Early customers communicate a venture's value and commitment to others; could support legitimacy and endorsement as a result distinct from sales.

paper: Zheng and Mai (2013) A Contextualized Transactive Memory System View on How Founding Teams Respond to Surprises: Evidence from China, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal 7(3)
why: Defines a surprise as an event founders see as unexpected and as significant for the startup, either opportunity or threat, and separates negative surprises; may give the general statement that outside events hit single startups.

paper: Grinvald (2011) Shaming Trademark Bullies, SSRN (law)
why: Open-access excerpt says small-business owners are easy prey for trademark bullies seeking exclusivity; would document incumbent trademark claims against small firms, though outside management journals.

paper: McAdams, Reynolds, Lewis and Patten (2001) When Bad Things Turn Good and Good Things Turn Bad: Sequences of Redemption and Contamination in Life Narrative, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 27(4)
why: Source definition of the redemption sequence: a bad scene in a life story turns good; ties it to benefit finding.

paper: Abonil, Shrivastava and Hyland (2023) Resilience and well-being among expatriate entrepreneurs: Envisioning life after a global crisis, Global Business and Organizational Excellence 43(2)
why: Passage: becoming entrepreneurs changed how participants viewed the COVID crisis; may state a crisis retold as a turning point for the better.

paper: Vogel and Bolino (2020) Recurring Nightmares and Silver Linings: Past Abusive Supervision, Posttraumatic Stress and Posttraumatic Growth, Academy of Management Review
why: Theorises silver linings (growth) from bad work episodes; matches gratitude for bad career episodes.

paper: Steigenberger, Cyron & Garz (2026) How Narrative Orchestration Helps Entrepreneurs Maintain Goals Despite Setbacks: The case of Star Citizen, Organization Studies
why: Abstract: narratives shift attention from obstacles to progress so that repeated setbacks do not cost legitimacy.

paper: Zettel (2025) Rethinking the rollercoaster: Resilience and affect in entrepreneurship, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal
why: Resilient entrepreneurs keep affect steady through venture challenges ('a train ride'); close to taking setbacks in stride, but about emotion, not narration. OA.

paper: Raffiee & Feng (2014) Should I Quit My Day Job?: A Hybrid Path to Entrepreneurship, Academy of Management Journal
why: Abstract: hybrid entry (keeping a day job) shapes entry and later survival; may state how the day job limits and shapes the venture.

paper: Yoon, Lee & Rhee (2025) Founder's entry strategy and funding performance in the crowdfunding industry: The mediating role of founder's attention, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal
why: Excerpt and abstract: hybrid and portfolio founders give the venture less attention than full-time founders, which lowers funding performance.

paper: Folta, Delmar & Wennberg (2010) Hybrid Entrepreneurship, Management Science
why: Foundational paper on keeping a day job while starting a venture; cited by Kappe et al. for the definition.

paper: Metzger, Meckler, Earle & Holloway (2024) Theorizing MacGyver: Entrepreneurial action in the face of environmental turbulence, Journal of Business Venturing Insights
why: Abstract: imposed opportunities under high time pressure and limited resources; may link time pressure to acting on what turns up.

paper: Ucbasaran, Westhead, Wright & Flores (2010) The nature of entrepreneurial experience, business failure and comparative optimism, JBV
why: Abstract: prior business failure shapes later entrepreneurs; for the 'lessons from failed ventures' strand.

paper: Eggers & Song (2015) Dealing with failure: serial entrepreneurs and the costs of changing industries between ventures, AMJ
why: Abstract: what serial founders carry from failed ventures into the next one.

paper: Unger, Rauch, Frese & Rosenbusch (2011) Human capital and entrepreneurial success: a meta-analytical review, JBV
why: Abstract: skills and knowledge relate to success more than years of experience; build-side human capital.

paper: Steyaert (2007) Of course that is not the whole (toy) story: Entrepreneurship and the cat's cradle, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Abstract: storytelling as a performance that balances complexity and coherence.

paper: King & Zeithaml (2001) Competencies and firm performance: examining the causal ambiguity paradox, Strategic Management Journal
why: Measures managers' own causal ambiguity about what drives their firm's performance; the nearest empirical version of 'we don't know why it worked'.

paper: Lippman & Rumelt (1982) Uncertain imitability: an analysis of interfirm differences in efficiency under competition, Bell Journal of Economics
why: Origin of the claim that even successful firms cannot identify the causes of their success.

paper: Jaskiewicz, Combs & Rau (2015) Entrepreneurial legacy: Toward a theory of how some family firms nurture transgenerational entrepreneurship, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Family narratives of past entrepreneurial achievements (legacy) are said to shape later generations' entrepreneurship; closest to 'heritage discovered later'.

paper: Mathias, Williams & Smith (2015) Entrepreneurial inception: The role of imprinting in entrepreneurial action, Journal of Business Venturing
why: Abstract: founders' early-life and family experiences imprint later entrepreneurial action; based on founders' own accounts.

paper: Bloom, Colbert & Nielsen (2021) Stories of Calling: How Called Professionals Construct Narrative Identities, Administrative Science Quarterly
why: Abstract: 'discerners' narrate a journey toward their destiny, one true calling; a narrative form like 'it was in my DNA', though not about entrepreneurs.

paper: White, Thornhill & Hampson (2007) A biosocial model of entrepreneurship: the combined effects of nurture and nature, Journal of Organizational Behavior
why: Abstract sets nature (heritable traits) against nurture (family business background) as causes of venture creation; a scholarly, not narrative, version of the theme.

paper: Toepler and Velamuri (2025) Legitimacy Building in Entrepreneurial Ecosystems: A Process Perspective for Sustainable Entrepreneurs, Managerial and Decision Economics 46(5)
why: Founder quote: after press coverage 'the network came to me'; may describe unsolicited contact and visibility from media attention.

paper: Aggarwal, Gopal, Gupta and Singh (2012) Putting Money Where the Mouths Are: The Relation Between Venture Financing and Electronic Word-of-Mouth, Information Systems Research
why: Blog coverage (eWOM by third parties) and venture financing; may state third-party coverage the firm does not control.

paper: Carare (2012) The Impact of Bestseller Rank on Demand: Evidence from the App Market, International Economic Review 53(3)
why: Causal effect of App Store top-rank display on next-day demand; a platform-side visibility shock outside the developer's control.
